meta.description: No — the real Steve Jobs never said it. It's a scripted line Aaron Sorkin wrote for the 2015 film "Steve Jobs," spoken by Michael Fassbender.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The musicians play their instruments. I play the orchestra'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the real Jobs — it's movie dialogue Aaron Sorkin wrote for the 2015 film "Steve Jobs." Wikiquote files it under Misattributed.

answer.label: Not Steve Jobs — a scripted line from the 2015 film
answer.sourceLine: This is a line of movie dialogue, not a documented Jobs quotation. It was written by Aaron Sorkin for the 2015 biographical drama Steve Jobs, spoken by Michael Fassbender’s Jobs in the backstage confrontation with Steve Wozniak before the 1988 NeXT Computer launch. There is no record the real Jobs ever said it — Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗, noting it “merely appears in the film.”

source.excerpt: The musicians play their instruments. I play the orchestra.
trail: The exact wording — “The musicians play their instruments. I play the orchestra” — appears in Wikiquote’s ‘Misattributed’ section for Steve Jobs ↗, flagged as merely appearing in the film with no real source.
It is dialogue from the 2015 drama Steve Jobs, written by Aaron Sorkin; as this analysis of the film confirms ↗, Jobs says it after Wozniak asks what he actually does.
The line is nonetheless widely reproduced as a genuine Jobs quotation on sites like Goodreads ↗, which credits it directly to Steve Jobs with no mention of the film.
source.excerptNote: In the film, Steve Wozniak presses Jobs on what he actually contributes when he can’t code or engineer, and Jobs answers with this conductor metaphor. The exchange comes in the film’s second act — the 1988 NeXT Computer segment, staged in an opera house — but it is Sorkin’s writing, not a quotation of the real Jobs.
source.rightsNote: The line is dialogue from the 2015 motion picture Steve Jobs, written by Aaron Sorkin (screenplay based on Walter Isaacson’s biography) and released by Universal Pictures. As a 2015 work it is firmly in copyright, held by the screenwriter and studio.

author.name: Aaron Sorkin
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.bio: Aaron Sorkin is an American screenwriter, playwright and director known for A Few Good Men, The West Wing, and his Academy Award–winning screenplay for The Social Network. He wrote the 2015 film Steve Jobs, structured as three real-time scenes before product launches, and has been candid that its dialogue and confrontations are dramatized inventions rather than transcripts of real events.

misattribution.heading: A movie line mistaken for the man
misattribution.intro: The quotation feels like vintage Jobs — visionary, a little arrogant — which is exactly why it spread as if he said it. In reality it was written for him, years after his death, by a screenwriter.

items.why: There is no interview, speech, or biography in which Jobs is recorded saying this. Wikiquote lists it as Misattributed ↗, noting it “merely appears in the film” and is “probably not based on a real source.”

The words are Jobs’s line in the 2015 drama Steve Jobs, delivered by Michael Fassbender in a fictionalized backstage scene — confirmed here ↗. Sorkin has openly described the film as an interpretation rather than a documentary.

misattribution.truthLine: The metaphor is memorable, but it’s Aaron Sorkin’s, spoken by an actor — not a sentence the real Steve Jobs is known to have uttered, per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why the mix-up happened
lead: Sorkin’s Steve Jobs was built as a three-act chamber drama, and this conductor metaphor lands as its thesis statement: Jobs’s genius wasn’t building the parts but orchestrating the people who did. That neat, quotable framing is precisely what made it travel — detached from the movie and re-pinned onto the real man.

Because the film dramatizes a real, recently deceased figure, audiences readily assumed the most striking lines were things Jobs actually said. They weren’t; they were an Oscar-winning writer’s interpretation of him.
context.pull: The line is the movie’s thesis about Jobs — written for him, not by him.
